1:
Clarke insists that Israel had taken no part of the country then belonging to Moab, only what had once been Moabite and had already been taken from them by Sihon; Wesley says the same, that the plains kept their old name though they had passed from Moab to Sihon and from Sihon to Israel. Ellicott fixes the ground, the Arboth Moab running from the house of wastes to the meadow of acacias in the upper Arabah, plains that had belonged to Moab and were now held by Israel after the victory over the Amorites. On the phrase rendered on this side Jordan he demurs, preferring alongside of the Jordan, since the Hebrew cannot settle which bank is meant — the Authorised Version renders the same form on yonder side in one clause of a later chapter and on this side in the next, and a prophet can describe Galilee as beyond Jordan. Clarke and Wesley are content with the east side, over against Jericho. Gill traces the route from Bashan, after the conquest of Og and Sihon, by way of the mountains of Abarim.

Keil and Delitzsch step back to see why the halt matters. Israel is encamped on the border of the promised land with only the Jordan between, and much had to be done before that line could be crossed. Two things in particular: the congregation was to pass a trial of great importance for all later generations, bearing on its relation to the heathen world; and Moses, forbidden Canaan for his sin at the water of strife, was to close the work of legislation before his death, issuing instructions for the conquest and the division of the inheritance and impressing the substance of the law once more on the people, that they might be kept from apostasy.

On the alarm that follows, the readers agree that it was groundless and disagree about how culpable. Henry points out that Moab had nothing to fear, since God had expressly forbidden Israel to contend with them and Moses had probably let them know it; they suspected the assurance was a sham to make them careless. So, notwithstanding the old friendship between Abraham and Lot, they resolved on Israel’s ruin and assumed without ground that Israel intended theirs — which Henry makes a rule, that those who design mischief pretend mischief is designed against them, their groundless jealousies colouring their causeless malice. He follows the reasoning: they hear of the victory over the Amorites and think their own house in danger when a neighbour’s is on fire; they observe the multitude and conclude the country will be licked up as an ox eats grass; so they feared where no fear was, and passed the fear to the elders of Midian, since if Moab fell Midian could not stand long.

Calvin reads the same alarm as a diagnosis. It shows, he says, what Scripture declares, that the reprobate are always agitated by groundless terrors, and that this is the just reward of men who do not seek peace with God, to be constantly harassed by wretched disquiet. God had exempted Moab by special privilege, and they invent causes of anxiety because they see God’s people overcoming great kings; as the sun’s brightness hurts weak eyes, so the blessings God gives the church torment the reprobate and stir them to envy. Calvin also frames the whole narrative: Satan turns every stone for the church’s destruction, and having failed by arms attacks by snares, while God turns every plot to his people’s salvation and makes his truth so victorious that it receives the testimony of its own professed enemies, as Balaam was made to proclaim it. Gill supplies the reasoning the rabbis attribute to Balak: if those kings could not stand before Israel, much less could he, the more so since they had already taken part of his country from him.
3:
Ellicott states the difficulty first: there was no ground at all for the apprehension, since the command given to Moses was to distress not the Moabites nor contend with them in battle. He is fair to Balak about it, however — it does not appear that he knew of the prohibition, the recent conquests naturally alarmed the whole nation, and there was an earlier refusal on Moab’s own part, when Israel asked leave to pass through the land and did not get it. Gill gives the same fear its dimensions, a panic that took in the king, the nobles and the people together, lest Israel should enter and treat them as Sihon and Og had been treated. Both he and Wesley then read the fright as a fulfilment rather than an accident: Wesley points to the general promise that the dread of Israel should be on all nations and to the particular prediction that the men of Moab would be seized by trembling, and Gill takes it as answering the same prophecy of Moses.

Keil and Delitzsch pass over the panic to the geography of the embassy, and admit defeat on the main point. Balak sent to Balaam at Pethor in Mesopotamia, and the town is unknown; a scholar’s attempt to connect it with a place south of Circesium and with a name in Ptolemy, and to identify both with Anah, they judge uncertain.

Who the elders of Midian were, and why Moab turned to them, is the second question. Gill reports two rabbinic accounts and does not choose between them: one Targum has Moab and Midian one people and one kingdom until this time, or at least long-standing allies, while another authority holds there was always mutual hatred and that Midian had come against Moab in war, peace being patched up only for fear of Israel — as Herod and Pilate were made friends in another case. He is firmer on the location: this was not the Midian where Jethro lived, on the Red Sea near Sinai, but a northern branch near the Arnon, both descended from Abraham’s son by Keturah. Wesley agrees and adds the titles these men carry elsewhere, kings of Midian in one place and princes of Midian in another, divided into their several kingdoms but united now by a common enemy, and a potent and crafty people who therefore made a natural confederate for Moab.

Ellicott raises a possibility neither of the others considers, that Balak himself was a Midianite imposed on the Moabites as king by their Amorite conquerors, and reads the closing words of the verse as marking a recent change of dynasty. On the figure of speech the commentators agree and explain differently. Ellicott finds the comparison well suited to a pastoral people who would think first of an ox at grass. Wesley glosses the verb as consuming and utterly destroying, the sense in which fire is said to lick up water and sacrifices, and takes the people round about to mean those living in the country adjoining each city where the princes resided.
5:
Who Balaam was is disputed before anything else. Gill runs through the rabbinic identifications and rejects them all — a magician in Pharaoh’s court when Moses was born; Laban the Syrian, which one Targum asserts; a grandson of Laban; Elihu who answered Job, on a tradition Jerome mentions — and denies the larger claim that Balaam was ever a good man or true prophet, since Scripture expressly calls him a diviner, a class abhorred of God. Wesley takes the opposite line on both counts. Balaam is called a prophet in the New Testament, he says, because God was pleased to inspire him to speak what follows; and many Jewish writers hold he had once been a great prophet, justly reckoned a man of interest with God because his predictions came true and his prayers were answered, though afterwards, for his covetousness, God departed from him.

The names are read differently too. Ellicott derives Balaam from a root meaning to devour, joined to the word for people, and his father’s name from a root meaning to consume, which has been thought to mark a family in which magic was hereditary; the variant form in the New Testament he explains from a pronunciation of the guttural. Wesley simply says the man had two names, as many others had. Ellicott also notes that Balaam is called the soothsayer elsewhere, one of a class not tolerated in Israel and named an abomination to the Lord.

Where Pethor stood produces a real dispute. Clarke reports a scholar’s objection that the description, far from being particular, fits any place in any country with a river, and adopts the remedy: twelve Hebrew manuscripts and two more confirm the Samaritan text in reading Ammon for his people, supported by the Syriac and Vulgate, so the clause should run by the river of the land of the children of Ammon — which he says necessity urges and which agrees with Deuteronomy. Ellicott keeps the received text and construes it instead, rendering it to Pethor which is by the river, even to the land of the children of his people; he places Pethor in Mesopotamia, where Lot had dwelt, and identifies the river as the Euphrates, called the river by eminence throughout the Old Testament. Wesley agrees, a city in Mesopotamia by the Euphrates, the river of Balaam’s own country. Keil and Delitzsch confess the town unknown, and Calvin cannot tell how the Chaldee interpreter came to place it where he does. Ellicott adds that covering the face of the earth is literally covering its eye.

Calvin turns from Balaam to the man who sent for him, and finds the case instructive because it begins well. The errors in which Satan entangles unbelievers, he says, are derived from good principles. Balak’s modesty deserves praise: conscious of his weakness and placing no confidence in human aid, he sets about imploring the help of God, which is our only safe refuge; so far he acts rightly, seeking to conciliate God’s favour and resting his hope of victory on God’s good will. The fault is in the route. Seeking God by circuitous ways he departs far from him, which Calvin calls the common error of hypocrites, that while they aspire after God they wander into indirect paths of their own. Balak wants deliverance but devises his own means, purchasing incantations from a mercenary prophet, and so subjects God to human inventions; he ought first to have asked what God willed and prayed in earnest faith, whereas he omits the main thing and is satisfied with a venal blessing. Some seed of religion was implanted in him, Calvin allows, and his reverence for the prophet is a sign of piety; but to try to win God over by vain inventions is foolish superstition, and to seek to put him under obligation is impious pride.
6:
Clarke opens by contradicting Gill’s verdict on the man. Balaam, he says, was once a prophet of the true God, and appears to have been one of that class of gnomic poets named earlier in the book, who had added the gift of sorcery or divination to his poetic one. He then supplies the belief the request depends on: prophets and sorcerers were supposed able to curse persons and places so as to confound their designs, frustrate their counsels, drain their strength and fill them with terror. Ellicott agrees that Balak undoubtedly believed in the efficacy of the incantations, and adds an observation borrowed from another commentator, that Scripture repeatedly celebrates it as a great favour to Israel that the Lord did not listen to Balaam but turned the curse into a blessing. Wesley paraphrases the request bluntly — use the utmost power you have with your gods to blast and ruin them — and catches the division of labour Balak proposes: you by your imprecations and I by my sword. Gill adds only that Balak is inviting the man to his country, his city and his court.

Clarke then leaves the verse for a long classical excursus. A Roman writer, he reports, has a whole chapter on the incantations used to induce the tutelary gods to abandon the cities they protected and to devote those cities and whole armies to destruction, and Clarke transcribes two of the ancient forms used against Carthage. The first, pronounced by the dictator or general and by nobody else at the opening of the siege, addresses whichever god or goddess had the people and city of Carthage in charge, and prays, beseeches and earnestly entreats that the deity forsake the place, leave its temples and sacred things, inspire the people with fear, terror and forgetfulness, and come over instead to Rome, where better temples and a more acceptable city are promised in exchange.

The gifts the messengers carry are read three ways. Ellicott records that the phrase is literally the divinations, notes that some take it to mean instruments of divination, and prefers the other sense on the strength of a parallel: as the word for glad tidings can also mean the reward given for glad tidings, so this word may mean not only divinations but the rewards of them. Keil and Delitzsch argue the same conclusion from two parallels rather than one, adding the word for work, which is regularly used for the thing wrought or the wages earned, so that the phrase here means the soothsayer’s fee. Clarke wants both. Whoever consulted a prophet took a present, since prophets lived on such gratuitous offerings; but more than a present is meant here, and he suspects it included everything needed to supply materials for the incantation, the drugs used on such occasions being often very expensive. His conclusion about the man is severe: Balaam was very covetous, loved the wages of unrighteousness, and probably lived by them.

On the embassy itself Gill and Ellicott note the same thing. Gill infers from the word elders that these were princes and nobles, and observes that men of both nations went, which shows that whether or not they were one people under one king they made common cause and joined in the same expedient to save their country. Ellicott says simply that the close alliance between the two nations appears throughout the whole narrative. Keil and Delitzsch add what happened at the other end: Balaam did not send the deputation away but told them to lodge the night at his house, so that he might bring them word what the Lord would say to him.
8:
The invitation to lodge is read as evidence of character, and read two ways. Gill takes it as showing that Balaam was at once inclined to do the work and would gladly have engaged in it if permitted; the night, he supposes, was when the man got his knowledge, whether by dreams, by familiar spirits, by consulting the stars or by other methods used at such hours — though it may also have been a device to gain time before giving a peremptory answer. Ellicott takes the same words as indicating the true character of Balaam from the other side: as a prophet of the Lord he must have known that in seeking to curse Israel he was sinning against the God who had chosen them. Wesley agrees that the night was the time God used to reveal his mind by dreams.

That Balaam names the Lord is agreed to be significant, and the motive is disputed. Clarke reads it plainly: it appears he knew the true God and had been in the habit of consulting him and receiving oracles from his mouth. Ellicott says only that this verse, with two later ones, shows the name of Jehovah was known to him. Wesley offers two motives and prefers the second. Balaam may have named the supreme God for his own greater reputation, as one who consulted no inferior spirits; or, more likely, because this was Israel’s own God, and the only possible way of ruining them was to engage their God against them — exactly as the Romans and other heathen, when besieging a city, used enchantments to call out the god under whose particular protection it stood.

Calvin uses the verse to settle what kind of figure Balaam was, and does it by distinguishing rather than by choosing a side. Since he waits for a revelation from the true God, it is probable he was not a magician or sorcerer whose power to divine came only from superstition or evil arts; the facts will show he was furnished with the gift of prophecy, however many impostures and deceptions he also used. But that does not put him among the true prophets God set over his Church, for the perpetual office of prophesying was never conferred on him and it was not joined to the office of teaching. Calvin then sets out what the genuine article was. God so directed those servants by his Spirit that they never spoke but out of his mouth; they did not foresee everything, only what was revealed, but nothing profitable was concealed from them, as the prophet said that the Lord does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants. They were the organs of the Spirit for every necessary prediction, so that the credit due to their prophecies was of an equable and constant character and they never spoke absurdly or in vain; they could adapt their prophecies to a just use, interpreting the Law once it was published, witnessing to grace in prosperity and to judgment in adversity, and ratifying the covenant by which God reconciles men to himself.

Balaam’s case, Calvin concludes, was far different. He and men like him were endowed only with a particular gift, so that they foretold some things truly and were mistaken in others, and uttered bare revelations with no admixture of doctrine. Yet God willed that such men should exist even among the heathen nations, so that some sparks of light might shine in their darkness and the excuse of ignorance be taken away. Keil and Delitzsch supply the outcome without comment: God expressly forbade him to go with the messengers and to curse the people, because they were blessed, and Balaam was obliged to send the embassy back without what it came for.
9:
Gill supposes the visitation came in a dream, as it did to Abimelech and to Laban, and Wesley has already said that the night was God’s usual time for such dealings. Neither treats the approach as extraordinary in itself; what is extraordinary is the man it comes to, since the narrative has just established that he was being paid to curse the people God had blessed. The question itself, however, is what the commentators dwell on, and they agree that it was not asked for information. Ellicott sets it beside two others of the same kind — the demand put to Elijah at Horeb, What doest thou here?, and the pair of questions put to Hezekiah after the Babylonian embassy, What said these men? and What have they seen in thine house? — and takes all three as calculated to rouse a slumbering conscience and open a man’s eyes to his own sin and danger. Wesley reaches the same conclusion by a slightly different route: the question was asked so that Balaam, by repeating the business in God’s presence, might be convinced and ashamed of the sin and folly of offering his services in such an affair, and so that there might be a foundation laid for the answer that follows.

Balaam’s reply is treated as a small test of honesty, and he passes it. Gill notes that he relates Balak’s message faithfully and exactly, word for word as the messengers had delivered it, and gives the reason: he knew well enough that he could not deceive an omniscient God or hide anything from him, however easily he might conceal the truth from men when it served his purpose. The observation cuts both ways — it credits the answer and impugns the habit.

Ellicott adds one point of rendering. Where the English has a people come out of Egypt, he would translate the people which came out from Egypt, and make the following verb singular with it: it covereth. The change is small but it turns an indefinite report into a definite one, the messengers naming a nation their master already knows of rather than describing an unfamiliar horde. It also brings the report into line with the wording Balak used when he first sent, so that Balaam is heard repeating the message rather than paraphrasing it — which is the point Gill had made from the other direction.
12:
Gill reads the prohibition as a plain refusal of the first thing Balak asked. Clarke reads it more narrowly. The command must mean that he was not to go with them to curse the people, since he afterwards went by God’s own direction; probably the words refer only to this first invitation, and in that sense Balaam obeyed them punctually.

Calvin takes the ground given for the refusal and builds a doctrine of the prophetic office on it. God removes any room for doubt by confirming the prohibition, because it was simply unlawful to curse those he had blessed. Nothing more is permitted to prophets, he says, than to be witnesses, ambassadors or heralds of a grace God bestows freely on whom he will; God is said to bless those he has embraced with favour and to whom he shows himself propitious, and he willed prophets to be his ministers in this while keeping the power altogether in his own hands. If they take to themselves the prerogative of blessing without commission, their act is not merely idle and ineffective but blasphemous — which is why the prophet convicts of falsehood those who by flatteries encouraged souls doomed to die and by threats slew those to whom God had promised life. Calvin draws two conclusions: it is vain for hypocrites to purchase pardon from men in order to propitiate God, and there is no need to fear degenerate ministers who domineer by virtue of their office even when they thunder against the innocent.

How honest the refusal was is then disputed. Calvin denies that Balaam’s obedience came from the heart. His words might deceive the simple by their air of humility — I will not go, because God forbids it — but he plainly indicates that he would undertake the journey if he were not forbidden; had his heart been sincere the honest answer was obvious, that it was useless to send for him or for anyone else, since Balak was setting himself against an inviolable decree. Had he given God the glory plainly, no second embassy would have come; his faltering excuse inflamed the foolish king’s desire instead, which is what he wanted, in order to raise his price. Ellicott makes a narrower version of the same charge: it does not appear that Balaam told the messengers the ground of the prohibition, that the people were blessed, and Balak accordingly hoped that stronger inducements would prevail. Keil and Delitzsch read Balak’s reaction the same way, and quote another writer’s two possibilities — that the king saw in the refusal the remains of a weakly fear of God, or simply a ruse to obtain better terms — adding that as a genuine heathen who saw in Israel’s God no more than the national god of that people, Balak thought gods as well as men could be made favourable by splendid honours.

Clarke alone defends him, and does it by rejecting a charge he first reports. A commentator he cites observes Satan’s practice of whittling God’s word away from hand to hand until it comes to nothing: Balaam told the princes less than God had told him, and they told Balak less than Balaam had told them, so that what reached the king was not the word of God but the word of man — simply that Balaam refused to come, with no hint that God had forbidden him. Clarke answers that in this Balaam is not to blame, since he told the messengers in the most positive terms that the Lord refused to give him leave to go with them, and could not have been more explicit. Gill notes the promptness at both ends: Balaam rose in the morning with the impression of the night still on him, and the princes went without attempting persuasion, seeing from his answer that it would be no use.
15:
Balak’s second attempt is read as a calculated escalation. Gill supposes the king thought Balaam had felt slighted, the earlier deputation being few and of the meaner sort, and so sent more men and greater, princes of the first rank, men of Balaam’s standing being highly revered. Henry sets the whole approach out as a strategy in three parts, and admires the persistence with a backhand: it would be well for us if we prosecuted a good work as earnestly and as constantly, in the teeth of disappointment, as Balak pursued this bad one. First, the messengers are more and more honourable, so that the diviner is treated with the deference due to a sovereign prince. Second, the request is urgent, a powerful king turning suitor and begging that nothing hinder him from coming — not God, Henry adds, nor conscience, nor any fear of sin or shame. Third, the terms are left open. Balak promises very great honour among the princes of Moab and then hands him a blank, undertaking to do whatever Balaam says; and Henry turns it round on the reader, that sinners stick at no pains and stoop to any humiliation to gratify their malice, so that we should be ashamed to be stiff and close-handed in complying with the laws of virtue.

Gill weighs what was actually offered. Where the first embassy baited his covetousness with presents, this one baits his pride with court preferment, making him perhaps a great officer or a chief minister; though one Jewish commentator reads the promise as wealth rather than office, on the strength of the doubled Hebrew phrase. Gill thinks both may be included, since honour and riches are alike weighty, desirable and ensnaring — and notes that Balaam himself seems to have heard money in it, since his answer speaks of a house full of silver and gold. Gill also observes that the great men did not decline the errand or think it beneath them to wait on a soothsayer.

Calvin reads the embassy as a study in the pride of superstition. However humbly ungodly men implore God’s grace, they do not lay aside their pride, as though their grandeur could dazzle God’s eyes; they think it enough to display magnificent ceremonies in order to make him comply, and whatever modesty superstition pretends, it always swells with a secret confidence. So Balak parades his dignity and power to obtain favour, and reckons that this will put Balaam at his service.

The reply is where the readers divide. Keil and Delitzsch take it at face value: Balaam could not transgress the mouth of the Lord to do little or great, and the inability flowed from a moral awe of God and a dread of his punishment, a conviction firmly established in his mind from beginning to end. Calvin allows the speech more spirit than the first answer and calls it noble and magnanimous in itself, then withdraws the credit. Why does Balaam not dismiss these unholy traffickers outright instead of entertaining them? He speaks in a spirit of boasting rather than to give God the glory, wanting the title and credit of a holy prophet from this parade of obedience; and by begging leave to enquire again what God’s pleasure is, he convicts himself of rebellion. He does not dare put himself forward openly to curse, which is so far well; but why, having been told plainly whether the thing was lawful, does he ask again? He is deliberating whether what God once prescribed must stand, and in effect asking God to deny himself by withdrawing his own decision. Once he had heard thou shalt not go, Calvin says, there was no pretext for continuing the controversy, and many still do the same, countermining a will of God they are fully assured of.
18:
Balaam’s famous answer is taken at two different valuations. Clarke gives it full credit: Balaam knew God too well to suppose he could reverse any of his purposes, and respected him too much to attempt anything without permission, so that covetous as he was he did not dare, under the double temptation of riches and honours, to go against the command. Clarke then turns it on the reader with a quotation, that many make all the professions of Balaam without justifying them by their conduct — pretending they would not do anything against the word of God for a house full of gold, and doing it for a handful. Ellicott offers both readings without deciding. The words may have been no more than an ostentatious semblance of disinterestedness and superiority to worldly considerations; or Balaam may genuinely have been conscious that he did not speak of himself, and that in his prophetic utterances he was only the mouthpiece of the Lord. Gill notes only that the men addressed were officers of state as well as princes of the land.

The request to stay another night divides them sharply. Clarke defends it as innocent: Balaam did not know but that God might make a further discovery of his will, and might therefore very properly seek more information. Gill treats the same words as self-condemning. The request shows a strong inclination to go and do what was asked if only he could get leave; otherwise he might and ought to have told the messengers at once that Balak need not have put himself and them to the trouble, since the thing was not in his power and he would not attempt it against the will of God, so that their best course was to go home directly. Instead he asks them to stay the night, which could only give them hope of succeeding. Ellicott is blunter still: Balaam knew that God is not a man that he should lie, nor the son of man that he should repent, and yet indulged the vain expectation that he might be allowed to curse those whom God had declared blessed.

Keil and Delitzsch pass over the motive and simply carry the narrative forward — the request to tarry, the night visit, the conditional permission, and the saddling of the ass in the morning — setting up the turn that follows, where God’s anger is kindled and the angel takes his stand in the way as an adversary.
20:
How the permission squares with the earlier prohibition is the question, and three answers are given. Ellicott denies any real inconsistency: the absolute and immutable prohibition had reference to the cursing, and the going with the messengers, forbidden in mercy at first, was enjoined in judgment at last — God often punishing disobedience to his declared will by letting transgressors eat the fruit of their own way and be filled with their own devices, giving them their request and sending leanness into their soul. Calvin says much the same in harder language. Balaam’s real desire, he says, was that God should belie himself, since a man persuaded of God’s truthfulness could hope for nothing but the same answer ten times over; so he lies to God in asking a permission that would convict God of caprice. God therefore ironically permits what he had forbidden. If it seems absurd that truth itself should speak deceptively, the answer is easy: God is guilty of no falsehood but looses the reins to a man obstinate in his own perverseness, as one might emancipate a wayward son who will not be ruled. Had covetousness not blinded him, Calvin adds, the meaning of an ironical permission would not have been hard to see; and hypocrites should learn from it that their pretences profit nothing, since God at length takes the wily in their own craftiness. Better by far to ask in simple teachableness what he would have us do and submit at once, without trying to alter a word or a syllable of what he has said — for to reopen what he has decided is to try to compel him by importunity to bend to our wishes.

The condition attached to the permission produces a sharper disagreement. Wesley states it plainly: on this condition he was to go. Clarke reports a grammatical argument that the condition was not in fact met. A scholar he cites observes that the Hebrew pronoun is sometimes used of a man doing a thing out of his own head without regard to another’s directions; and since Balaam was to go only if the men came in the morning to call him, and instead was too hasty and went to them, the text says not simply that he went but that he went of his own head, uncalled — and in this, on that reading, his iniquity chiefly lay. Ellicott renders the same clause the other way. The words may be given as since, or forasmuch as, the men have come to call thee, since the messengers had already come for that very purpose, as an earlier verse states with the same verb. On his construction the condition is not a test left hanging but a fact already accomplished.

Gill sides with the first reading by observation rather than grammar: Balaam rose early and did not wait for the princes to call him, which showed how eager he was to be gone and how intent on the journey. Clarke closes with the general reflection the episode suggests to him, that many are restrained from sinning merely by fear of God — they would gladly do the evil, and wish the thing were not forbidden, because the desire for it is strong.
22:
Calvin puts the difficulty as a question: how can God be angry when Balaam had so far attempted nothing against his command? His answer is that God apparently permits much he does not approve — flesh in the wilderness, the writing of divorce, several wives at once, none of them right — and that Balaam sinned by pertinaciously urging what was sinful, deserving death though God mitigated the sentence. Henry states the principle without the examples: sin is not less provoking because God permits it, and we must not conclude that because providence does not restrain a man God approves the thing, for he suffers sin and is angry at it still. Henry adds a second reason, that nothing displeases God more than malicious designs against his people, since he who touches them touches the apple of his eye.

Gill assembles four grounds. The permission was conditional on the princes calling him, and he went uncalled; he had not told them, any more than the first embassy, that God had forbidden the cursing, which would have ended the journey; he went with a positive will to curse, which must displease a God who knew his heart; and the leave itself had been given in anger, so a man who took it might expect some mark of displeasure. He quotes a rabbi to the same effect, that Balaam saw the thing was evil in the Lord’s eyes and desired it anyway. Wesley makes the first ground the whole of it — Balaam went of his own accord, not waiting to be called, but rising and calling them — and cites the apostle’s verdict, that he ran greedily into an error for reward. Ellicott finds the same fault in the tense: the words are literally because he was going, a participle marking the continuous act, so that the man deliberately and resolutely proceeded on his journey in defiance of the warnings he had received.

Calvin then faces the objection that the punishment seems ill-proportioned. The prophet who, having faithfully delivered his message, ate bread on the way back at another prophet’s instigation, falling only through carelessness, was punished with death, while this impostor, who prostitutes his tongue for hire and would sell the grace of the Spirit, is merely terrified with threats. Here, he says, the temerity of the flesh would gladly find fault with God; but the punishment awaiting Balaam, which he did not finally escape, was delayed in order to display God’s glory more brightly, and when the reason for God’s works is not apparent the doubt should be repressed at once.

On the angel the readers are agreed and vary in emphasis. Ellicott would render the verb as placed or stationed himself in the way. Henry sees the fulfilment of the promise that God would be an enemy to Israel’s enemies, holds that the holy angels are adversaries to sin and perhaps employed in preventing it more than we know, and adds the comfort that no attempt is formed against God’s people without angels sent to break it; and he observes sharply that this angel was Balaam’s adversary only because Balaam counted him so, such interventions being in truth our best friends. Wesley says the angel came to oppose him if not to kill him. Calvin fastens on the humiliation: the angel had assumed a body a brute could see, yet to the prophet’s great disgrace the glory was revealed first to the ass while his own eyes were shut. Henry and Wesley both notice the small detail of the escort. The princes had probably gone ahead or by another road, leaving Balaam with his two servants — honour enough, Henry remarks, for such a man, who needed no promotion from Balak; and Wesley notes that those times had more simplicity and less ceremony, so it is not strange he travelled behind with only his own men.
23:
That the beast saw what the prophet did not is the point everyone starts from. Gill says Balaam’s eyes were held by the power and providence of God so that he might be rebuked by his own ass, to which God gave sight he withheld from her master; the man had little reason after that to boast of visions and revelations, or that he was the one whose eyes were open. Clarke generalises the phenomenon rather than the humiliation: when God granted visions, those particularly concerned saw them while others in the same company saw nothing, as happened to the men with Daniel and to the men with Saul on the Damascus road. Gill also reads the drawn sword as more than a threat — it signified not only that Balaam deserved to die but the death he would actually die, by the sword, as he did.

The ground itself is described with some care. Keil and Delitzsch take the second station to be a pass among the vineyards with walls on both sides, so that the animal, terrified, pressed against the wall and crushed her rider’s foot; the third is a pass so narrow that there was no room to move to right or left, and being unable either to turn aside or to squeeze past, the ass threw herself down. Ellicott would render the second place the hollow pass of the vineyards, and the barriers fences rather than walls. Gill supposes she got into the narrow path before Balaam could turn her back, a footpath between the vineyards where there was no room for man and beast to pass without great difficulty and danger. He also settles a small question of continuity: the angel seems not to have been always in sight, but to have disappeared as he moved from place to place and to have stood visible again at each new station, which is why the ass is said to see him three separate times while her master never does.

Clarke draws the sequence into a lesson, quoting a commentator who reads the angel’s three positions as the stages of God’s judgments against sinners. First he mildly shakes his rod at them and lets them go untouched; then he comes nearer and gives an easy correction, as it were wringing their foot against the wall; and when all this proves ineffectual he brings them into such straits that they can turn neither to the right hand nor to the left, but must fall before his judgments if they will not turn fully to him. The reading takes the increasing narrowness of the road as the argument, which is what the narrative itself emphasises: a field to escape into, then a wall on either side, then nowhere at all.
28:
The commentators all treat the speaking ass as the point where the narrative must be defended, and they defend it differently. Clarke relocates the wonder: had the ass opened her own mouth we might well be astonished, but when God opens a mouth an ass can speak as well as a man. He notes that Balaam himself shows no surprise, because he saw it was the Lord’s doing; and he declines to rehearse the heathen stories of animals given speech, not thinking it proper to occupy the reader’s time with fictions. Gill occupies it at length. He grants the affair extraordinary, since a creature without organs for speech spoke plainly and distinctly, and answers that there is no need to think it incredible, for what cannot omnipotence do — so there is no need either for the Jewish expedient of making the whole thing visionary and never literally performed. He then argues that the pagans can hardly object, given their own reports: the ass that carried Bacchus over a river and was rewarded with a human voice, which Gill suspects was a fable framed from this very story; the horse of Achilles given speech by a goddess; an ox that spoke, among the wonders the ancients reported.

Calvin answers the sceptics on principle rather than by parallel. Their objection, that there is a great difference between an ass’s bray and an articulate voice, looks plausible, and he meets it with a question: whence would men have speech at all, unless God opened their mouths at the creation, and how do magpies and parrots imitate a human voice unless God willed to show in them some extraordinary power? Who then will impose a law on the Maker of the world forbidding him to adapt the mouth of a beast to words — unless one supposes him bound, having once appointed an order in nature, never to display his power by miracles? He presses further: if the ass had been turned into a man we should have had to revere the proof of an incomprehensible power, and it is strange to call it a fable when we are told only that a few words were drawn from her; and if unclean spirits utter words in spectral illusions, why should God be unable to endow mute tongues with speech?

What exactly the ass was given divides two of them. Wesley says God conferred on her the power of speech and reasoning for that time. Calvin denies the second half of that expressly: the words were drawn from her without intelligence or judgment, as a sound of any kind might be diffused through the air.

Ellicott takes on the modern version of the objection, that the incidents were subjective impressions rather than outward events, and answers with two arguments. First, consistency requires the whole narrative be read one way, so that if the voice was an impression on Balaam’s mind the angel must have been one too — and then subjective to the ass as well, which raises a greater difficulty than it removes, since an impression produced in a beast’s mind crosses the line between intelligent and brute creation further than articulate speech does. Second, the real question is not whether the results could have been produced that way but what the narrative itself suggests and what the apostle’s words require; the text gives no hint that its parts are to be read differently, and no statement could be couched in terms more directly suggestive of a literal fact than that the dumb ass, speaking with man’s voice, forbade the madness of the prophet. Calvin adds the reason for the method: God might have rebuked Balaam directly by the angel’s words, but the reproof would not have been severe enough without gross ignominy, and so he appointed a beast to instruct him.
29:
The word Balaam uses of his beast is disputed. Gill would rather render it defiled me than mocked me, since she had run him against a wall and lain down with him in the dust; one version has it that she rolled him in the dirt. He finds the sense of mocking hard to understand here, because only his own servants were present and he can hardly have been troubled at being exposed to them; and he suggests as an alternative that the word may mean seeking occasion, so that the charge is of looking for a chance to throw him and do him harm or kill him. Keil and Delitzsch render it that the ass had played him ill.

Balaam’s composure under the miracle is explained rather than admired. Wesley notes that he was not much terrified by the ass speaking, and offers two reasons: perhaps he was used to conversing with evil spirits who appeared and discoursed with him in the shape of such creatures, or perhaps he was so blinded by passion that he never considered how strange the thing was. Either way the answer he gives is furious rather than astonished — a wish for a sword and a threat to kill her — which is itself the reply to those who have thought the absence of surprise an objection to the story.

The ass’s second speech is where the argument turns. Keil and Delitzsch summarise it as a plea from long service: she had been ridden by him from far back and had never been used to behave this way, and Balaam was obliged to admit it. Those words of an irrational beast, whose truth he could not deny, made an impression on him and roused him from his blindness, so that God could now open his eyes and he saw the angel. Gill marvels at the exchange itself, that she made a reply as though she understood what was said to her, and so had the faculty of reasoning and discoursing as well as of speech.

Ellicott works on the phrase for the length of that service. It is literally ever since thou livedst, that is, all thy life long, and two Targums paraphrase it as riding from thy youth to this day; he supports the plausibility of so long a service by an Arabic report, quoted from Gill’s commentary, of an ass its owner rode for forty years. He then takes the closing phrase, unto this day, and turns it to a use outside this chapter altogether: its occurrence here throws light on such passages as the note in Deuteronomy that a place was called after a man’s own name unto this day, and shows that the formula does not necessarily imply any long interval between the event and the writing.
31:
What had been wrong with Balaam’s sight is settled first. Gill mentions the possibility that he had been struck blind, as the men of Sodom were, but prefers that his eyes were merely held: he could see other objects, his own ass among them, and only the angel was hidden from him, as Elisha’s servant could see the besieging host but not the chariots and horses of fire until his eyes were opened. Gill puts it as a veil rolled away, or the removal of whatever had by God’s power and providence hindered the sight.

Calvin draws a general principle out of that. Whatever the acuteness of our senses, it is not only implanted by God but sustained or extinguished by his secret working; Balaam’s eyes are opened, so there had been a veil before them keeping him from what was plain, and God at his pleasure dulls the senses of men who think themselves very acute, since perception is his particular gift. He then makes the episode a mirror of how hypocrites fear God — only while his presence weighs on them, for as soon as they can get away they revel like runaway slaves. Balaam bows and worships because a drawn sword is over him and vengeance is impending, but the fear produces no real correction. He confesses that he has sinned and shows some fruit of repentance in offering to go home, yet betrays a servile and compulsory fear that trembles at nothing but punishment. His plea that he did not know the angel stood in the way admits as much: unless the angel had been armed to punish him he would have gone on in perfect security. And the offer to turn back if it displease thee exposes the craft, since he knew perfectly well already that it displeased God; the condition is ridiculous, a pretence of doubt about something abundantly clear. What use is it to say I have sinned, Calvin asks, if a man thinks he may still prosecute the journey he began against God? Where God’s will is positively known we are to have recourse to no crooked subterfuge that delays performing it. Wesley reads the prostration simply as a token of reverence and submission.

The angel’s charge is rendered two ways. The English calls the way perverse, and Ellicott would translate instead that the way leads to destruction in my sight, which turns a moral verdict into a warning about where the road ends. Wesley keeps the moral sense and names the root: the perverseness sprang from covetousness. Gill notes only that the angel spoke once Balaam had risen and was standing before him.
33:
The verse is grammatically awkward and two commentators say so. Keil and Delitzsch reject the traditional rendering — unless the ass had turned aside, surely I had slain thee — as indefensible by the rules of the language, and read instead a broken-off sentence: perhaps she turned out before me, for otherwise I should surely have killed thee and let her live. On that construction the angel does not state why the ass turned aside at all. He hints at it lightly and leaves Balaam to gather the rest — that the animal turned from affection to her master, with some dim foreboding of the danger threatening him, and that for that very service of love, as though it were her wages, she had been beaten. Ellicott adopts the same reading and says so, allowing that there may be a broken construction here and referring the reader to the other commentator by name.

Clarke and Wesley take the plain sense and draw the moral from it. Wesley reads the angel’s words as saying that Balaam alone would have been killed and the ass spared, so that her turning aside and falling down were wholly for his benefit and not her own, which makes his anger against her unjust and unreasonable. Clarke widens it into a reflection: how often the meanest animals and the most trivial occurrences are the instruments of preserving our lives and saving our souls, since the messenger of justice would have killed Balaam had God’s mercy not turned the ass out of the road. Gill puts the same point in a sentence — the ass saw the angel when Balaam did not, that was why she turned, it was well for him that she did, and he should not have struck her.

The three readings agree on the substance and differ on what the angel is doing with it. On the traditional rendering he states a fact about what would have happened; on the reading Keil and Delitzsch prefer he supplies a fragment and lets the man complete it, which fits the rest of the scene, where Balaam is not told what he has done so much as shown it.
34:
The confession is weighed and mostly found short. Gill limits it narrowly: Balaam is confessing that he sinned in beating the ass, not that he is sensible of his covetousness, of the evil disposition of his mind, or of his wicked intention in going with the princes to curse Israel if he could and collect Balak’s presents and preferments. Clarke reads the same words far more generously. Here, he says, is proof that though Balaam loved the wages of unrighteousness he still feared God, since he is willing to drop the whole enterprise if God is displeased with it; and he turns the point on his readers, that the piety of many called Christians does not extend so far, for they see that a thing displeases God and proceed anyway.

The permission that follows is read by everyone as judicial rather than indulgent. Gill calls it no command but a concession, or rather a bare permission, leaving Balaam to go if he would, suffering him to follow his own heart’s lusts and giving him up to them for his own destruction — adding that it was never the going as such that displeased God, but the going with such an intention. Ellicott says the same, that the earlier command is here repeated and the unrighteous prophet punished by being made to reap the fruit of his own perversity; and he notices in passing that the angel identifies himself with the one who sent him, since he says that the word I shall speak is what Balaam must speak, where the earlier verse had God saying it. Wesley states it as terms: I allow thee to go, on the following conditions.

Calvin returns to the irony he had found in the first permission and then guards it against misuse. Balaam was so conscious of his own covetousness that he knowingly deceived himself rather than being deceived; his claim to be going by God’s command was a mere pretence, and God was casting derision on a wicked man’s pertinacious folly rather than approving what, in words, he permitted. Calvin then states the distinction the case requires: God did not approve what he condemned, and yet chose that it should be done, for even when he executes his purpose through wicked men he does not prescribe to them that they should act so. He illustrates from two reigns. God willed that Solomon should be punished by the hand of Jeroboam and that vengeance should fall on the house of Ahab by Jehu; yet it was not right in Jeroboam to overturn what God had declared about David’s posterity, and Jehu, though anointed by a prophet, was guilty in seizing the kingdom, since nothing but ambition drove him. So here, God willed to prove by Balaam’s own mouth how effectual and unchangeable his determination about the adoption of the people was, so that his truth and faithfulness might be more conspicuous; and Balaam sinned all the same, drawn like a hound by the scent of gain to sell his curses for money. Keil and Delitzsch record without comment that Balaam went with the princes of Balak.
36:
Henry reads the meeting as a study in mismatched expectations between two confederates. Balak has no doubts at all now that Balaam has come, and goes out to meet him at the very border of his country, partly from impatience to see a man he expected so much from and partly to do him honour and so engage his utmost power. Henry turns that into a reproach: see what respect heathen princes paid to men who had only the name and face of prophets, and how welcome one was whose mouth was full of curses, while the ambassadors of Christ are so little respected and those who bring tidings of peace received so coldly. Ellicott corrects the place-name to the city of Moab and renders the border clause as the Arnon flowing at its extremity, Sihon having taken the Moabite territory as far as that river; Keil and Delitzsch identify the town on the northern boundary as probably the old capital, reduced to a frontier post for the same reason. Wesley notes only that the place was not far from the camp of the people Balak wanted cursed.

The king’s complaint is where the readers part. Henry hears offended dignity: Balak thinks himself slighted by the delay, since he had used importunity and had honours in his gift, and delay looked like judging those honours not worth accepting. Henry allows the appeal some force, since promotion is a tempting bait, and turns it into a question: it would be well if we were drawn into God’s service by the honour he sets before us, so why delay, and is not he able to promote us?

Calvin uses the same speech to expose the temper of superstition. Those who are devoted to their superstitions without a sincere fear of God cringe to their prophets and all but worship them, yet inwardly cherish a pride that breaks out when it is least expected. The king goes out to pay honours to the prophet’s office, a condescension equivalent to laying crown and sceptre at his feet; but the dissimulation shows the moment he expostulates and boasts of the riches with which he could reward him, as if the prophetic office were subservient to money and its revelations commanded by wealth. Calvin generalises: however servile the flattery superstitious men pay their idols and priests, they never lay aside their proud spirits, and if a priest will not gratify his worshippers they inveigh against him as bitterly as against a swineherd.

Balaam’s reply is read three ways. Clarke calls it a noble resolution faithfully kept, since he wished to please the king and gain wealth and honour and would not displease God even for such prospects; many who slander this prophet, he adds, have not half his piety. Henry finds it doubtful rather than noble — Balaam warning the king not to depend too much on him, gladly cursing Israel if only he might. Calvin allows that at first sight it breathes nothing but piety and then reads it as a diplomat’s answer: Balaam signifies that so far as civility required and so far as it depended on himself he would have complied with the king’s wishes, and pleads his office only as the one thing that prevents him. Keil and Delitzsch note the tactical purpose, an attempt to lower expectations the king had formed from his coming at all; and they add that he said nothing to Balak he had not said to the messengers, concealing the same part of the truth from both. Gill puts the sense of the opening words shortly: let nothing more be said of what is past.
39:
What Balak was doing with the oxen and sheep is disputed. Gill offers both possibilities. The verb may mean he slew them for sacrifice, Balak himself acting as priest, as kings commonly did, with Balaam brought in to observe and explain any omen, as a seer did for the chiefs of Greece; or, more likely from the words that follow, it was a feast — though it may have been both, since part of an idol offering was usually eaten in a festival way, after the manner of the peace offerings. Ellicott renders it as slaughtered, noting the word need mean no more than to slay though it is commonly used of sacrifice, and thinks Balak most probably made a sacrificial feast and sent portions to Balaam and the princes; kings, he adds, not infrequently acted as priests of old, instancing Melchizedek and a line of Latin verse about a king who was also priest of Apollo.

Keil and Delitzsch settle what the sacrifices were for and to whom. They were not so much thank-offerings for Balaam’s safe arrival as supplications for the success of the enterprise, which they argue from the place and the time — not offered where the two men first met, and offered only on the eve of the great event. Nor were they offered to the Moabite idols, from which Balak expected no help, but unquestionably to the God of Israel, whom he wished to draw away from his own people and secure for the Moabites. Clarke reaches the same conclusion less confidently, that the sacrifice was to gain the favour of Balak’s gods and perhaps to propitiate the Lord as well. The site of the town they cannot fix, since it is named only here, though it cannot have been far from where they went next morning.

Calvin reads the whole reception as a technique. Moses records how sumptuously Balaam was received — a city of streets, animals slaughtered in abundance, guests invited to banquet with him — and the object was that he should be enticed until ashamed to refuse anything to a king who had treated him with such liberality, as though he stood in God’s place or the grace of God were marketable.

The choice of the high place divides them. Gill and Wesley take it as a place of worship, consecrated to Baal — the Targum names it the idol Peor — and Gill reckons it was chosen both for the view and because it was a site of religious observance. Calvin agrees and draws the conclusion: Balak brought him to what was in effect a temple, the better to conciliate God’s favour, from which it appears that Balaam had no fixed views about the service of God but worshipped promiscuously among the heathen, whether sharing their superstitions or making no difficulty about any rite that would curry favour — there having always been trimmers who corrupt religion for flattery’s sake. Keil and Delitzsch deny the religious motive outright: Balak took him there not because the place was consecrated to Baal but because it was the first height on the way to the plains from which the camp could be seen.

How much of the camp came into view is a further question. Clarke and Wesley both suppose the object was to have the whole people in sight, Clarke because Balak feared a curse might not reach the unseen, Wesley because he hoped the sight of so great a host would rouse the prophet’s passion. Ellicott gives both readings: on one construction of a later verse Balaam saw the whole army even to its extremity, though the verse is more commonly taken to mean he saw only the outermost part, as the Targum has it, the camp of Dan which went at the rear.
